# Wounds and Trauma
## Trauma types
- [color=#ff5c5c]Ballistic[/color] — deep wound, external or internal bleeding, and possible organ, bone, nerve, or tendon damage. - [color=#ff5c5c]Puncture[/color] — narrow deep wound with a high chance of vascular or organ damage. - [color=#ff5c5c]Slash[/color] — open wound that can damage vessels, tendons, and nerves. - [color=#ffcc66]Blunt[/color] — bruising, fractures, and internal structural damage. - [color=#ffcc66]Explosive[/color] — multiple localized injuries and systemic trauma. - [color=#ffcc66]Thermal[/color] — burn or cold injury to tissue. - [color=#ffcc66]Electrical[/color] — local injury and cardiac rhythm stress. - [color=#ffcc66]Chemical[/color] — tissue damage and systemic toxic burden. - [color=#ffcc66]Barotrauma[/color] — injury caused by pressure change.
## Wound data
- body zone and surface; - depth and severity; - open, treated, or healed state; - capillary, venous, arterial, or internal bleeding source; - contamination, infection stage, and necrosis; - dressing, packing, pressure, and tourniquet treatment; - healing progress and scar state; - embedded foreign body and exit wound.
## Structural injuries
- [color=#58e6d9]Bone[/color] — fracture state, stability, displacement, and fixation requirement. - [color=#58e6d9]Joint[/color] — stability, dislocation, and movement restriction. - [color=#58e6d9]Tendon[/color] — integrity, movement, and grip. - [color=#58e6d9]Nerve[/color] — sensation, motor function, and neural interface. - [color=#58e6d9]Organ[/color] — structural integrity and functional capacity.
## Wound progression
1. Contamination increases infection burden. 2. Infection progresses through contaminated, local, deep, organ, systemic, and sepsis stages. 3. Deep infection produces necrosis. 4. Movement and repeated trauma can reopen a wound. 5. A healed severe wound can leave a scar.
Use the [color=#58e6d9]Wounds[/color], [color=#58e6d9]Regions[/color], and [color=#58e6d9]Organs[/color] tabs to select treatment.
